title: Erik Prince Team Pitched White House on El Salvador Detention Camp Plan
description_short: Politico reported that Erik Prince’s team pitched a proposed El Salvador detention and deportation operation; no approval was established.
description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors pitched the White House on a plan involving a 10,000-person detention camp and transportation for as many as 100,000 people. The article describes a proposal, not an approved contract or an operating program, and says White House interest was unclear.
description_long: On April 11, 2025, POLITICO reported that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors were pitching the White House on a proposal connected to deportations to El Salvador. The proposal described gathering as many as 100,000 people from U.S. prisons, holding them in a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador. It said Prince’s group, partnering with El Salvador, would handle the logistics and would need access to government immigration files held by law-enforcement agencies to determine people’s immigration status. The proposal claimed a contract would help resolve legal issues and improve the government’s ability to locate, capture, detain, and deport immigrants; those were claims in the pitch, not legal findings. An administration official expected the proposal to be discussed during Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s planned White House visit. Prince and the White House declined to comment. POLITICO also reported that an LLC called 2USV was registered in Wyoming, which the article described as an indication that Prince’s group hoped to move to a more serious phase of pitching. The report describes proposed terms and a contractor pitch; it does not report an awarded contract or say the camp or flights began.

title: Trump Orders Increased Transfers of Federal Assets to Local Police
description_short: Executive Order 14288 directs an increase in transfers of excess federal military and national-security assets to local law enforcement.
description_medium: On April 28, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14288, directing the Attorney General and Defense Secretary to increase provision of excess military and national-security assets to state and local law enforcement within 90 days. It also orders a review of covered police consent decrees. A July opinion column relayed the Legal Defense Fund’s concerns about aggressive policing and accountability; completed transfers and effects were not established.
description_long: On April 28, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14288, “Strengthening and Unleashing America’s Law Enforcement to Pursue Criminals and Protect Innocent Citizens.” The order directs the Attorney General and Secretary of Defense, consulting the Secretary of Homeland Security and other appropriate agency heads, to increase the provision of excess military and national-security assets to state and local law enforcement within 90 days. It also directs Defense, coordinating with the Attorney General, to determine how assets, training, non-lethal capabilities and personnel could be used to prevent crime. Separately, the Attorney General is directed to review covered police consent decrees and related measures and modify, rescind or seek to conclude those judged to unduly impede law-enforcement functions. These are agency directives, rather than a record of completed transfers or concluded decrees. A July 2025 Times-Republican opinion column relayed the Legal Defense Fund’s concerns that the order could promote aggressive policing and make accountability more difficult. The column’s concerns describe potential effects rather than documented misconduct.

title: Trump Ends Canada Trade Talks and Announces a 10% Tariff Increase Over Ontario’s Reagan Ad
description_short: Trump said he was ending trade talks with Canada over Ontario’s Reagan ad and announced an additional 10% tariff, without specifying affected goods.
description_medium: On Oct. 23, 2025, Trump called Ontario’s Reagan ad “FAKE” and said he was ending trade negotiations with Canada. The next day, he suggested to reporters that the ad might have used AI, a claim not established by the sources. On Oct. 25, he announced an additional 10% tariff on Canada over the ad; Reuters reported that the affected goods were not specified.
description_long: Ontario’s provincial government aired a television advertisement using excerpts from former President Ronald Reagan’s 1987 radio address about tariffs. FactCheck.org found that the ad rearranged parts of the address and omitted context, but did not change Reagan’s broader anti-tariff message. On Oct. 23, 2025, Trump called the ad “FAKE,” said it was intended to interfere with pending Supreme Court tariff litigation, and announced that he was ending trade negotiations with Canada. The following day, he told reporters, “I guess it was AI or something”; this was an attributed suggestion, not evidence about how the advertisement was produced. On Oct. 25, Trump announced an additional 10% tariff on Canada, citing the ad. Reuters reported that he did not specify which goods the increase would cover and that most Canadian exports were exempt from tariffs under USMCA. Ontario Premier Doug Ford had said the province would pause the U.S. ad campaign on Monday after discussions with Prime Minister Mark Carney so trade talks could resume. The report specified neither an effective date for the additional tariff nor the later outcome of the negotiations.

It described at least four officers whose promotions were delayed or canceled because they had previously worked for former Joint Chiefs chair Gen. Mark Milley, citing officials. The report also described specific personnel cases: Adm. title: EPA Rescinds Methane Standards for Oil and Gas Production and Processing
description_short: EPA’s August 2020 rule rescinded methane standards for oil and gas production and processing and removed transmission and storage from the rule.
description_medium: On August 13, 2020, EPA issued final policy amendments to oil and gas New Source Performance Standards. The amendments removed the transmission and storage segment from the rule and rescinded methane standards for production and processing segments. EPA presented the changes as reducing compliance burdens on the industry.
description_long: On August 13, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency issued final policy amendments to the New Source Performance Standards for the oil and natural gas industry. The amendments removed the transmission and storage segment from the standards, rescinding both volatile organic compound and methane requirements for that segment. They also rescinded methane standards for production and processing while retaining volatile organic compound standards for those operations. EPA argued that the methane requirements for production and processing duplicated existing controls and provided no additional health protections; that was the agency’s rationale for the change. The policy rule accompanied separate technical amendments addressing leak monitoring and repair schedules, recordkeeping, reporting and other compliance requirements. Together, EPA presented the rules as simplifying compliance and reducing industry burdens. The policy amendments were later disapproved through a joint congressional resolution signed into law on June 30, 2021, and ceased to be in effect.

title: EPA Denied a Petition to Ban Chlorpyrifos in 2017
description_short: On March 29, 2017, EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt denied a petition to revoke chlorpyrifos food tolerances and cancel its registrations.
description_medium: On March 29, 2017, EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt denied a petition to revoke all food tolerances for chlorpyrifos and cancel its registrations. Pesticide Action Network North America and the Natural Resources Defense Council filed the petition in 2007. EPA said questions about neurodevelopmental effects warranted further evaluation during registration review.
description_long: On March 29, 2017, EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt signed an order denying a petition seeking to revoke all chlorpyrifos food residue tolerances and cancel the pesticide’s registrations. Pesticide Action Network North America and the Natural Resources Defense Council had filed the petition in September 2007. Food tolerances determine the permitted pesticide residues in food; their revocation would affect food uses of chlorpyrifos. The denial reversed the course of EPA’s October 2015 proposal to revoke all food residue tolerances. In explaining the decision, EPA said that questions concerning potential neurodevelopmental effects remained unresolved and warranted further scientific evaluation during registration review. Pruitt emphasized regulatory certainty for farms using the insecticide, while the order deferred a final registration review decision on retaining, limiting or removing it from the market. The action therefore left the petition’s requested restrictions unadopted in 2017 while EPA continued its review of the pesticide and its potential health effects.

title: EPA Relaxes Coal Ash Monitoring and Closure Requirements in 2018
description_short: On July 18, 2018, EPA finalized coal-ash amendments allowing conditional monitoring exemptions and giving some disposal units more time to close.
description_medium: On July 18, 2018, EPA finalized amendments to its 2015 coal-ash disposal regulations. The changes allowed permitting authorities to suspend groundwater monitoring where evidence showed no potential for hazardous constituents to reach the uppermost aquifer. They also changed groundwater protection standards and gave certain units triggered into closure additional time to stop accepting waste. EPA presented the amendments as added flexibility for states and utilities.
description_long: On July 18, 2018, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized its first amendments to the 2015 federal regulations governing coal ash from electric utilities and independent power producers. The changes affected requirements for coal-ash landfills and surface impoundments, including groundwater monitoring and the timing of closure. Under one alternative performance standard, an approved state permitting authority, or EPA where it issued permits, could suspend groundwater monitoring if evidence demonstrated no potential for hazardous constituents to migrate to the uppermost aquifer during operation and post-closure care. Another permitted technical certifications instead of certification by a professional engineer. EPA also revised groundwater protection standards for constituents without established federal drinking-water limits. The rule provided additional time to stop receiving waste and initiate closure for certain units, including unlined impoundments with elevated groundwater contamination and units failing the aquifer location restriction. Acting Administrator Andrew Wheeler described the action as giving states and utilities more flexibility.

title: Bolton Reorganizes NSC Global Health Security Unit
description_short: Bolton’s 2018 NSC reorganization eliminated a standalone global health directorate; reporting said related duties remained elsewhere.
description_medium: John Bolton’s 2018 reorganization of the National Security Council eliminated its standalone Global Health Security directorate. The Los Angeles Times attributed the decision to Bolton and reported a streamlining rationale. TIME reported that an administration official said the directorate’s responsibilities were absorbed elsewhere, while critics said removing its senior leadership reduced attention to global health security.
description_long: In 2018, National Security Adviser John Bolton reorganized the National Security Council and disbanded its standalone Directorate for Global Health Security and Biodefense. The Los Angeles Times reported that the team had coordinated health agencies, the State Department and the Pentagon in preparations for disease threats. An NSC spokesman described the change as an effort to reduce bureaucracy and streamline offices with similar missions, while saying the administration remained committed to pandemic preparedness. TIME reported that Tom Bossert left when Bolton took charge in April 2018, and that Rear Admiral Timothy Ziemer, who headed the health team, left in May. An administration official told TIME that the directorate’s responsibilities had moved into another NSC directorate and that related expertise remained on the council under different titles. Critics quoted by TIME argued that removing the senior director role weakened White House attention to global health security. The administration and its critics therefore offered competing assessments of the same organizational change.
